conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be part of your care team. I understand you came in after having thoughts about driving into a tree. Can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… I was driving and just felt this wave of sadness. I thought, ‘Just hit the tree and end it.’ But I didn’t do it. I told my psychiatrist this morning and she said to come here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for sharing that. It takes courage. Are you having those thoughts now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not right now. I just feel numb. I’ve been through ECT before, but they’ve been tapering it down and I think that’s making things worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Given your history and recent thoughts, the psychiatry team wants to keep you here for monitoring while we arrange your next steps, including ECT.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I guess I need it. My veins are really bad though—getting IVs is a nightmare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I see that. Because you’re going to need regular treatments, we’re planning to place a port-a-cath. It’s a small device under the skin that makes access easier and less painful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. Is that a surgery? Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a minor procedure, done with sedation. You’ll be comfortable. It usually takes about an hour. We’ll schedule it early next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds better than getting stuck every time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll also keep you on your current meds—gabapentin, omeprazole, tramadol, levothyroxine, and trazodone. Lithium was in your list, but your level this morning was low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been taking it, but maybe it’s not enough. My mood’s been slipping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The psychiatry team is starting you on 150 mg at night. We’ll check levels and may increase it. It can help stabilize your mood over time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll take it. I just want to feel stable again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs came back—everything looks stable. Blood count, kidneys, thyroid—all normal. Your urine test showed methadone, but you’re not on it, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I haven’t taken methadone. Maybe it’s a false positive? I only take my prescribed meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’ll note that. No concerns otherwise. How’s your abdominal pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but it’s chronic. I think it’s from endometriosis. Tramadol helps a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on gabapentin and tramadol for now. The team mentioned possibly weaning tramadol long-term, but that’s not now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d rather avoid opioids, but I need something for the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll work with you on that. For now, your priority is mental health stabilization.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your lithium level came back at 0.3, which is low. Psychiatry wants to increase your dose to 300 mg at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe? I’ve heard lithium can have side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll monitor your levels and kidney function. At the right dose, it’s very effective for bipolar disorder.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust the team. I just want to feel like myself again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a heads-up—your port placement is scheduled for tomorrow morning. The radiology team will confirm the placement with a chest X-ray after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. Will I be asleep?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get sedation, so you’ll be very relaxed and won’t feel pain. You might remember bits, but mostly you’ll just sleep through it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds okay. I’m just nervous about recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have some soreness and swelling, but it usually improves in a few days. We’ll keep the site clean and check it daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back. The port was placed successfully. The chest X-ray confirms the tip is in the right spot—near your heart where it should be.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, good. It’s sore, but I can deal with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There’s some swelling and mild tenderness, which is normal. We’ll keep the dressing on for now and change it tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be able to use my arm okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, just avoid heavy lifting for a few days. You’ll get instructions on care before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your follow-up labs look good. Hemoglobin improved, electrolytes stable. Lithium level pending.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I’ve been feeling a little more present. Still flat, but not as dark.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. The ECT is scheduled for Thursday. Being here helps ensure you’re medically stable for it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about ECT, but it’s helped before. I just hate the memory fog.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor you closely. The benefits often outweigh the side effects, especially when mood is severely affected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Lithium level is back—0.6, which is better. Still a bit low, but moving in the right direction. We’ll keep you on 300 mg nightly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been sleeping better since the dose went up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Trazodone and the lithium are likely helping. Any nausea or tremors?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, nothing like that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Your port site is healing well—less swelling, no signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tomorrow’s your ECT. After that, you’ll be transferred to Deaconess 4, the psychiatric unit, for continued care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m ready for the next step. I feel safer here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad to hear that. You’ve made real progress. We’ll keep you on all your current meds, including tramadol for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the lithium stays at 300 mg?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for now. The psych team will follow up on levels and adjust if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You had ECT this morning—went smoothly. You’re awake, alert, and oriented. No complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a little groggy, but okay. My head doesn’t hurt.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal. The grogginess should pass in a few hours. Your port site is healing well—just mild tenderness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’m glad it’s in. Makes things easier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re discharging you to Deaconess 4. They’ll continue your psychiatric care, including ECT and medication management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Will I keep the same meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—gabapentin, omeprazole, tramadol, levothyroxine, trazodone, and lithium 300 mg at night. We’re also adding hydroxyzine for anxiety if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds good. And my mom will be my contact?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we have her as your contact. You’re alert, walking on your own, and medically stable. We’re confident you’re ready for the transfer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I feel like I’m on a better path now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve worked hard this week. Keep reaching out when you need help. That’s how we stay ahead of these episodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I don’t want to go back to that place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re not alone in this. The team at Deaconess will support you. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in before transfer. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: More clear-headed. Still tired from ECT, but okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. You’re doing well. The port is secure, your labs are stable, and your mental status is clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go. I feel safer knowing I’ll keep getting treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad. You’ve made real progress. The team at Deaconess will continue your care plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m hopeful this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hope is important. Keep using your tools—meds, therapy, and reaching out. You’ve got this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you doing well soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all we ask. Rest up before transfer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will be in with discharge instructions and your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good luck.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too.
